column5: unquenched fire and dead rebels
column6: Isaiah leaves the rebels as corpses while their worm does not die and their fire is not quenched; 87:13 makes the sufferer himself unable to die, so the bodily condition is the pointed difference within the shared enduring-fire scene.

column5: Gehenna gloss, soul not dying, unquenched fire
column6: Targum Jonathan's Gehenna paraphrase turns Isaiah's displayed corpses into sinners whose soul does not die while their fire is unquenched; that Jewish interpretation comes unusually close to the commentary's conscious, unending state in the fire.

column5: Gehinnom consumed but certain sinners remain
column6: In its reading of Isaiah 66:24, the Bavli says certain apostates descend to Gehinnom for generations and that Gehinnom is consumed while they are not; it explicitly develops the asymmetry of lasting punishment without the punished passing away.

column5: enter life or Gehenna's unquenchable fire
column6: Jesus contrasts entering life with being cast into Gehenna's unquenchable fire; that direct life/fire antithesis sharpens the commentary's claim that the fire of 87:13 is a place where the condemned does not live.

column5: worm does not die, fire not quenched
column6: Mark retains Isaiah's imperishable worm and unquenched fire; it is a close Christian formula for punishment that never runs down, alongside the commentary's renewed torment and never-arriving death.

column5: people seek death but cannot find it
column6: In an apocalyptic plague people long to die, but death flees them; this is a direct, though temporary, counterpart to the commentary's picture of agony in which death is wanted or approaches yet never arrives.

column5: fire, everlasting smoke, no rest day or night
column6: The worshippers of the beast are tormented and have no rest day or night; its denial of repose closely meets the commentary's expansion of not dying into no easing, sleep, or stillness.

column5: conscious anguish in flame
column6: The rich man remains conscious and cries out that he is in anguish in flame; this supplies a narrated Christian analogue for the commentary's insistence that fire's occupant is not extinguished by suffering.

column5: fixed chasm, no passage out
column6: Abraham describes an impassable chasm that prevents passage from the place of torment; it specifically parallels the commentary's repeatedly frustrated desire to leave the fire.

column5: eternal punishment and eternal life
column6: Matthew's final judgment places eternal punishment and eternal life in one antithetical sentence, a close frame for the commentary's contrast between enduring torment and the real, lasting life denied to it.

column5: lake of fire called the second death
column6: Revelation names the lake of fire the second death, whereas 87:13 carefully says that its inhabitant does not die there; the contrast shows two different theological ways of naming fire's finality.

column5: resurrection body enduring eternal fire
column6: Augustine argues that the damned can suffer bodily fire without their bodies being destroyed; this patristic explanation directly addresses the commentary's problem of pain persisting while death never completes.

column5: longing for death that does not come
column6: Job describes sufferers who dig for death but do not find it; although it is not a hell scene, the denied release provides a concrete analogue for the commentary's death withheld amid affliction.

column5: death spoken of as sleep
column6: Jesus calls Lazarus's death sleep before explaining that Lazarus has died; it closely supports the commentary's secondary sense of death as sleep and rest, which is unavailable in the fire.

column5: the dead in the Lord rest from their labors
column6: The blessed dead are said to rest from their labors, furnishing the positive counterpart to the commentary's claim that the one who cannot die in the fire is also denied rest.

column5: dead do not live, shades do not rise
column6: Isaiah says of hostile rulers that they are dead and will not live or rise; the negative Hebrew life verb closely matches the life/death language, but punishment here is exclusion from resurrection rather than 87:13's deathless suffering.

column5: your dead shall live and arise
column6: Isaiah's answer to the preceding no-life statement is that God's dead will live and arise; it supplies the positive resurrection horizon against which the commentary distinguishes a fire that grants neither death nor life.

column5: awakening to everlasting life or contempt
column6: Daniel's sleepers awake either to everlasting life or everlasting contempt; this gives a biblical two-outcome resurrection frame for the commentary's opposition between full afterlife and enduring punitive condition.

column5: martyr's resurrection to life and tyrant's exclusion
column6: The martyred brother expects resurrection to life from God but tells the persecuting king that he has no resurrection to life; its death-to-life contrast illuminates the commentary's peaceful death-and-rising figures over against the doomed state.

column5: the living one became dead and lives forever
column6: The risen Jesus names himself the living one who became dead and is alive forever; this compact death-life-resurrection sequence is the positive inverse of 87:13's suspended condition.

column5: raised Christ dies no more
column6: Paul says that the risen Christ dies no more and death no longer rules him; it provides a Christian account of deathlessness joined to actual life, precisely the conjunction the commentary says hell lacks.

column5: in Adam all die, in Christ all made alive
column6: Paul binds Adam to universal death and Christ to being made alive; this directly meets the commentary's Adam-to-earth sequence of death and eventual resurrection, rather than an ultimate state without either.

column5: no more death in the renewed creation
column6: In the new creation death, mourning, crying, and pain are removed together; it supplies the positive destination in which no death means healed life, contrasting with the fire's deathlessness without life.

column5: Arabic h-y-y and m-w-t, Hebrew hayyim and mavet
column6: Moses sets life and death before Israel and commands them to choose life; the Hebrew life/death pair is cognate with the Arabic roots named in the commentary and makes ethical response determine which side is inhabited.

column5: turn from the wicked way and live
column6: God calls the wicked to turn from their way and live; this closely parallels the commentary's moral reading in which turning from the reminder yields a final state without life.

column5: rejected call, later cry unanswered
column6: Wisdom's hearers refuse her call and later call out without answer; it gives a specific biblical form to the commentary's warning that remembrance and a request for release come too late.

column5: instruction is your life
column6: Proverbs calls disciplined instruction life itself; this makes a precise Jewish counterpart to the commentary's claim that accepting the admonition is a response to what gives life.

column5: hearing the word, passing from death to life
column6: The one who hears and believes Jesus' word has eternal life and has passed from death to life; it directly parallels the commentary's spiritual use of life for a person who receives the warning.

column5: dead in transgressions, made alive with Christ
column6: Ephesians says those dead through transgressions are made alive with Christ; it offers a concrete Christian use of death and life as present moral-spiritual conditions beneath the commentary's final outcome.

column5: dead while living
column6: The self-indulgent person is said to be dead while living, a Christian moral metaphor that resembles an in-between state; the commentary instead stresses that 87:13 negates both exits without calling its victim merely half-dead.

column5: not hearing Moses and prophets
column6: The rich man's requested warning is refused on the ground that those who do not hear Moses and the prophets will not be persuaded even by resurrection; it joins refused warning to an irreversible postmortem setting as the commentary does.

column5: teaching as rain and speech as dew on grass
column6: Moses compares teaching to rain and speech to dew upon grass; this directly links the commentary's rain-and-living-pasture imagery with admonition that nourishes rather than the fire that consumes.

column5: rejected Torah, stubble consumed by fire
column6: Isaiah joins rejection of YHWH's Torah to roots rotting and stubble consumed by fire; its warning, vegetation, and fire form a particularly close triad beside the commentary's avoidance of reminder and grass-to-fire imagery.

column5: Spirit placed in the dead so they live
column6: God promises to put his spirit in Israel's dry bones so that they live; it is the positive prophetic counterpart to the commentary's layered account of life as more than continued sensation.

column5: Torah-hearer as a watered fruitful tree
column6: The person who meditates on Torah is like a tree by streams that bears fruit; this gives the commentary's admonition, flourishing vegetation, and living-versus-barren moral contrast a biblical form.

column5: grass withers but God's word stands forever
column6: Isaiah contrasts withering grass with the enduring divine word; it clarifies the commentary's movement from short worldly life and fading pasture toward what is lasting.

column5: life of this world and bliss of the world to come
column6: Rabbi Jacob compares the whole life of this world with the superior bliss of the world to come; this is a close rabbinic counterpart to the commentary's contrast between preferred near life and the more abiding life.

column5: gaining the world and forfeiting one's life
column6: Jesus asks what profit comes from gaining the whole world while forfeiting one's life; it gives a sharp Gospel analogue to the commentary's claim that preferring the near life forfeits the true one.

column5: the life that is truly life
column6: Paul urges storing treasure for the future in order to seize the life that is truly life; its explicit distinction between apparent present possession and real life closely matches the commentary's account of the enduring afterlife.

column5: earth, dust, and return to dust
column6: Adam is told that he came from dust and will return to it; this grounds the commentary's contrast between earth as the place of ordinary life and death and fire as the place where neither transition occurs.

column5: aged couple and an improbable promised child
column6: Abraham and Sarah are old and Sarah's fertility has ceased when a child is promised; this ancestral annunciation pattern stands beside the commentary's aged Zechariah and barren wife receiving Yahya.

column5: Zechariah's prayer, son, and name John
column6: Gabriel answers Zechariah's prayer with a son who must be named John; it is the direct New Testament scene corresponding to the commentary's Yahya annunciation.

column5: Yahya wordplay and the Greek name Ioannes
column6: Luke gives the child the Greek name Ioannes, representing Hebrew Yohanan, rather than a form meaning he lives; the shared prophet therefore preserves the narrative but not the commentary's specifically Arabic Yahya/yahya wordplay.

column5: John grows and becomes strong in spirit
column6: Luke describes John as growing and becoming strong in spirit; this is a focused New Testament counterpart to the commentary's Yahya commanded to take the Book with strength.

column5: be strong in keeping the Torah
column6: Joshua is told to be strong and courageous in observing all the Torah; this biblical command supplies a close scriptural pattern for the commentary's phrase about Yahya taking the Book with strength.

column5: John righteous and holy
column6: Herod recognizes John as a righteous and holy man; this bears on the commentary's portrayal of Yahya as given purity and set against the tyrannical, rebellious figure bound to the fire.
